A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RouteFinder. Their complete main texts and Appendices A–C are readable, including equations, tables, and figures. Renamed models and reorganized material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original routing experiments, component ablations, mixed-backhaul adaptation experiments, and CVRPLIB evaluations in Section 5 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, expanded component and reward-normalization ablations, adaptation results, and an encoder-representation analysis.

M1.justification: v2 adds RF-TE with pre-normalization, RMSNorm, and SwiGLU, extending v1's instance-normalized, post-norm ReLU architecture. It also introduces per-variant reward normalization in the POMO gradient. Mixed Batch Training, global embeddings, and EAL's zero-extension procedure remain; FlashAttention was already documented in v1.

E1.justification: Both versions retain 16 training variants, eight mixed-backhaul adaptation variants, and the same 32 CVRPLIB X instances. Within this coverage, Appendix A.1 broadens distance-limit conditions from a fixed default of 3 to sampled feasible limits, introducing variation in constraint tightness.

E2.justification: Table 5.1 reduces the separately reported MVMoE and MVMoE-L alternatives to one MVMoE baseline. The mixed-backhaul comparison drops the finetuning-only control and adds OR-Tools, while retaining zero-shot, from-scratch, and Lin et al.'s adapter method. MTPOMO becomes an explicit component-ablation reference.

E3.justification: Appendix A.1 revises the reported distance-limit generation procedure. Adaptation evaluation switches from RF-POMO/RF-MoE-L to RF-TE, and new experiments compare normalization rules and smoothing factors. The new t-SNE study uses 100 instances per variant at size 100. Main training budgets and greedy augmented evaluation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 expands the two-component ablation to four components, adds normalization sensitivity experiments and layerwise t-SNE analysis, and explicitly evaluates adapter initialization. It removes v1's training-stability curves and replaces adaptation learning curves with initialization and final-result tables, changing the evidence about convergence.

E5.justification: v1 Table 5.2 reports uncertainty values, Figure 5.1 specifies three independent runs and displays shaded variation, and Listing 1 supplies a seed. v2's replacement figures and tables omit corresponding uncertainty, repeated-run, and seed information. This establishes reduced reporting, not that fewer runs were performed.

E6.justification: Table 5.1 substantially replaces objectives, gaps, runtimes, and rankings. Table C.2 replaces RF-POMO's 14.972% average gap with RF-TE's 12.303%, while MTPOMO's reported average changes from 16.114% to 30.202%. These involve revised configurations, not controlled cross-version gains. v2 also adds numerical adaptation results and contains inconsistent entries, including 350.808 in Table 5.1.

T1.justification: v2 adds definitions of cumulative and exponential reward averages and a normalized policy-gradient expression in Equations 4–6, plus RF-TE layer equations in Appendix B.2. These extend the mathematical specification; the underlying VRP formulation, EAL construction, and environment constraints remain, without new theorem or proof results.

C1.justification: v2 makes the transformer encoder and reward normalization core contributions alongside the retained framework and adaptation mechanism. The introduction strengthens the empirical claim from competitive performance to more than 10% gap reduction across all variants, and the conclusion asserts superiority over state-of-the-art neural baselines.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving reward-scale balance, encoder stability, representation separation, and MoE inference costs. Appendix C.3 qualifies v1's broad generalization interpretation: compositional training now worsens MTPOMO, with sampling differences suggested as a reason. The conclusion removes explicit asymmetric-routing and autoregressive-scaling limitations.

D1.justification: Table B.1 preserves most hyperparameters from v1's Hydra listing while adding RF-TE options and removing configuration class paths. v2 specifies the chosen normalization factor, t-SNE implementation and perplexity, and AL licensing. Hardware, reported training times, and code-access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds UNCO and expands discussion of supervised multi-task solvers. Additional references support the encoder, reward normalization, t-SNE, and future decomposition/search directions. The principal positioning relative to MTPOMO, MVMoE, and Lin et al.'s adapters remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, experimental narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Section 4 reorganizes existing embedding and sampling material into Model and Training subsections. Appendix configuration material moves into B.4, the appendix contents page disappears, and author information is revised.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the framework overview, adds an encoder comparison diagram, replaces the ablation table with bar charts, and replaces adaptation curves with a results table. It adds a six-panel t-SNE figure and converts the configuration listing into a hyperparameter table, alongside broader typography and layout changes.

improvement.justification: Expanded ablations and explicit adapter-initialization results strengthen component-level evidence. However, v2 removes uncertainty reporting and the finetuning-only control, while Table C.2 repeats optimal values as MTPOMO objectives despite positive gaps. Its blanket 10% claim is also not uniformly supported: CVRP-50 reports 1.226% for the best RF versus 1.242% for MVMoE. These conflicting gains and losses in validation prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
